cereal-or-granola-bar-kelloggs-nutri-gra.title: Cereal or granola bar (Kellogg's Nutri-Grain Cereal Bar)

content.title: About
content.content: Kellogg's Nutri‑Grain Cereal Bar is a ready‑to‑eat snack made from whole grains, dried fruit and a light sweet syrup. It is marketed as a quick breakfast or on‑the‑go snack, providing energy and a modest amount of protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Nutri‑Grain bars were first introduced in the early 1990s as part of Kellogg's fast‑breakfast lineup.
The formula combines whole grains (wheat, rice) with dried fruit, making it more nutritious than typical candy bars.
Each bar is individually sealed in a moisture‑proof wrapper for convenient portability.
The product is promoted as a "breakfast on the go" and targets both children and active adults.
In some markets, versions are fortified with additional vitamins and minerals such as iron and vitamin D.

items.title: Source of whole grains
items.content: Whole grains provide complex carbohydrates that release energy slowly, helping maintain satiety.

items.title: Modest protein content
items.content: Each bar supplies about 3–4 g of protein, supporting muscle repair after light activity.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains B1, B2 and B6 vitamins, which aid normal metabolism.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Dried fruit and whole grains add fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Convenient and portable
items.content: Individual packaging makes it easy to snack without preparation.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Bars contain added sugars, so intake should be limited for those monitoring blood glucose.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: May contain gluten, soy, and dairy, which are important for people with food allergies.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: One bar provides roughly 120–130 kcal; consider total daily calories when incorporating into the diet.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: A small amount of salt is present, which may be a concern for individuals with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bar can be eaten straight from the wrapper, sliced into yogurt, oatmeal or smoothies, or taken as a convenient snack during travel, school or workouts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, consume within 3–5 days for best quality.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑fat butter crackers are light, crisp biscuits made from whole‑grain flour, vegetable oil and a modest amount of salt. They have a delicate buttery flavor, a crunchy texture, and fewer calories than regular butter crackers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The lower fat content is achieved by using low‑density vegetable oils and incorporating air‑binding agents.
These crackers are popular as a diet‑friendly snack and as a side for soups and salads.
Whole grains such as wheat, rye or oats are often included, boosting dietary fiber.
The product is marketed as a healthier alternative to traditional butter crackers.

items.title: Reduced fat content
items.content: Lower fat levels help decrease overall calorie intake, supporting weight management.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain base provides fiber that promotes regular digestion.

items.title: Provides complex carbohydrates
items.content: Crackers deliver slow‑release energy, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole grains supply thiamine, niacin and folate, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Reduced salt makes the snack more suitable for people monitoring blood pressure.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: These crackers usually contain wheat, so they are not suitable for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Some varieties may include artificial flavors or preservatives that could trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Potentially high glycemic index
items.content: Large portions may raise blood sugar, especially for people with diabetes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crackers can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, served with soups, salads, dips, or used as a base for canapés. They are convenient for on‑the‑go meals or work breaks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in an airtight package. For extended shelf life, keep refrigerated to preserve crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Cucumber (Cucumis sativus) is a long, cylindrical, green-skinned fruit native to South Asia, eaten as a vegetable. It has crisp, watery flesh and a mild, refreshing flavor. Cucumbers are eaten raw in salads, sandwiches, and drinks and are also pickled.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cucumbers are about 95 percent water.
Botanically, cucumbers are fruits, related to melons, squash, and pumpkins.
Cucumbers have been cultivated for thousands of years.
Pickles are cucumbers preserved in brine or vinegar.
Cucumbers are often eaten with their skin and seeds, which contain much of the fiber and nutrients.

items.title: Very hydrating
items.content: Cucumbers are mostly water, making them refreshing.

items.title: Provides vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K supports normal blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Contains plant compounds
items.content: Cucumbers contain flavonoids and other compounds with antioxidant properties, especially in the skin.

items.title: Very low in calories
items.content: Cucumbers are low in calories and make a light snack.

items.title: Bitterness
items.content: Some cucumbers contain bitter compounds called cucurbitacins. Discard cucumbers that taste very bitter.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Cucumbers may cause gas or burping in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people, especially those allergic to ragweed pollen, may experience itching or tingling in the mouth.

items.title: Wax and residues
items.content: Wash cucumbers thoroughly, since conventionally grown ones may have wax or residues on the skin.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cucumbers can be sliced into salads, sandwiches, and yogurt sauces, eaten with dips, or blended into chilled soups and drinks. They can be pickled in brine or vinegar. Eating them with the skin on gives more fiber.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cucumbers in the refrigerator, wrapped in paper or in a breathable bag in the crisper drawer, where they usually keep for about a week. Very cold storage can cause pitting and softening. Cut cucumber should be stored in an airtight container and eaten within a couple of days.

content.title: About
content.content: Fried shrimp are a seafood product made from boiled or raw shrimp that are then deep‑fried until golden and crispy. They have a tender, slightly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. Fried shrimp are often served as an appetizer, added to salads, pastas, rice dishes, and sushi.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp belong to the crustacean family and are close relatives of lobsters and crayfish.
There are more than 2,000 shrimp species, but culinary use focuses on tiger, northern, and king shrimp.
Frying in oil preserves most of the protein while adding a rich flavor.
Shrimp can change color from gray to pink depending on the cooking method.
In Japan, fried shrimp are frequently served with soy sauce and wasabi.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Shrimp provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, making them an excellent source of high‑quality protein.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When fried moderately, the fat content remains low and is mostly polyunsaturated.

items.title: Source of iodine and selenium
items.content: Iodine supports thyroid function, while selenium has antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nervous system health and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids in shrimp help lower triglyceride levels.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Potential toxins
items.content: Improperly stored or undercooked shrimp can harbor bacteria and toxins.

items.title: High sodium in processed products
items.content: Pre‑packaged fried shrimp are often salted; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fried shrimp hot as a snack, add them to salads, pastas, rice bowls, tacos, or use them in sushi. They are easy to eat by hand, peeling off the tail, and the meat can be lifted from the shell with a fork.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fried shrimp in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a zip‑top bag at –18 °C. Before eating, check for any ammonia‑like or off odors.

spinach-frozen-cooked-with-butter-or-mar.title: Spinach, frozen, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen spinach is a leafy vegetable that is blanched, cooled and flash‑frozen shortly after harvest. Cooking it with butter or margarine adds a smooth flavor and helps absorb fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: When frozen quickly after picking, spinach retains most of its vitamins and minerals.
Blanching before freezing kills most bacteria and preserves the bright green color.
Spinach belongs to the Amaranth family and is a close relative of Swiss chard.
In the United States frozen spinach is a common ingredient in casseroles, lasagnas and smoothies.
Spinach is rich in lutein, which supports eye health.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin A and beta‑carotene
items.content: Supports vision, immune function and skin.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron is needed for oxygen transport in the blood, especially important in plant‑based diets.

items.title: High in folate
items.content: Folate is involved in DNA synthesis and is crucial during pregnancy.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Food allergies
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergic reaction to spinach.

items.title: Sodium content in prepared dishes
items.content: If butter or margarine is salted, consider the overall sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thaw the spinach and quickly sauté it with butter or margarine, then add to soups, sauces, omelets, casseroles, or use as a filling for pies. A small amount of fat helps retain nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen spinach in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once thawed, use within 1–2 days and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator.

vegetables-stew-type-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Vegetables, stew type, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed vegetables with no added fat are a blend of various vegetables gently cooked in their own juices. Cooking without oil preserves the maximum amount of vitamins, minerals, and natural flavors, making the dish light and nutritious.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stewing retains more fiber compared to frying.
Common ingredients include carrots, broccoli, bell peppers, and zucchini.
Stewed vegetables can serve as a base for soups, stews, and side dishes.
The absence of added fat reduces the calorie count, which is useful for diet plans.
Slow cooking keeps the vegetables’ natural color and aroma.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Vegetables provide vitamins A, C, K and B‑complex, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: They contain potassium, magnesium and iron, essential for heart and muscle function.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: No added fat makes the dish suitable for weight management.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients in vegetables help combat free radicals.

items.title: Allergy to specific vegetables
items.content: Some individuals may react to certain vegetables such as tomatoes or peppers.

items.title: Nutrient loss with overcooking
items.content: Excessive stewing can diminish heat‑sensitive vitamins like vitamin C.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Vegetables like spinach and beetroot are high in oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stones in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stewed vegetables can be served on their own, added to salads, used as a filling for wraps, or as a side to meat and fish. They reheat well in the microwave or on the stovetop.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked stewed vegetables in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer keeping, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 3 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Greek Yogurt with Oats is a thick, creamy yogurt made by double‑straining, to which whole oat flakes are added. The product combines protein‑rich yogurt with the fiber‑filled goodness of oats, providing a balanced snack or breakfast addition.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats contain beta‑glucans that help lower cholesterol levels.
Greek yogurt typically has 2‑3 times more protein than regular yogurt.
The yogurt‑oat combo delivers long‑lasting satiety.
Oats are one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown for over 10,000 years.
Greek yogurt is often used as a substitute for sour cream or mayonnaise in recipes.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Greek yogurt provides about 10 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Oats are high in soluble fiber, which promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The yogurt delivers a substantial amount of calcium essential for bone health.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Greek yogurt contains live cultures that help maintain a balanced gut microbiome.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: Unlike many flavored yogurts, this product contains minimal added sugar.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals with lactose intolerance or a casein allergy should avoid this product.

items.title: Sugar content in flavored versions
items.content: While plain oats are not sweet, some varieties may contain added sugars.

items.title: Caloric density in large portions
items.content: The combination of yogurt and oats can be calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy it as a standalone snack, blend into smoothies, use as a base for desserts, mix with granola, or top with fresh fruit. The oat flakes add a hearty texture and extra nutrition.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. Do not freeze, as the yogurt texture may change.
